note: Files: s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r5/day1_hard328-01/{abaybektursun-1114-151534-e72c (base cue), abaybektursun-1114-151540-86ef (RL plain)}/answers.jsonl, the same S3 objects the recipe names, stored at runs/theory-tests/<job>/answers.jsonl instead of runs/theory-rows/ because this task says to fetch there. Each file has 328 rows, one per problem_index, so the first-in-file-order rule removes nothing. The text field includes the 3 prefilled cue tokens (' line!\n\nOkay') for the base and starts the same way for RL. They fall in decile 1, which the statistic does not use. The filter is n_generated >= 12000 with cap hits included. Deciles are taken by character, the regex is used as written (case-sensitive; 'I' and 'me' count as whole words; re.findall returns non-overlapping matches), r = (M8+M9+1)/(M2+M3+1), statistic.median takes the mean of the two middle values for an even count, and the statistic is median(base) - median(RL). If either file has fewer than 5 kept rows, the script prints refuted_without_number. Refuted_by is coded as measured > -0.15. n = base kept rows + RL kept rows. Bootstrap: one entry per problem kept in either file, as a pair (r_base or None, r_rl or None), so the resample is paired by problem. If a resample happens to contain no kept row for one model, that model's full-sample median is used for that resample (a fallback I added; it is rare when both groups have at least 5 rows). Other reading (alt_measured): the length filter on n_new instead of n_generated. In these rows n_generated is n_new or n_new + 1 (mean difference 0.77 tokens for the base, 0.94 for RL), so the two readings differ only at the 12000 boundary. Possible errors: deciles are by character, not by token, as the recipe says. RL's long answers on hard328 may be few, which makes the RL median noisy. example_row has its text and prompt cut to 300 characters, with their full lengths given in text_len and prompt_len.

File: the base cue job abaybektursun-1114-151534-e72c answers.jsonl (S3 path as in inventory.md, stored at runs/theory-tests/). It has 328 rows, one per problem. Kept rows have n_generated >= 12000, cap hits included. The text is split on '\n', each line's start offset is the sum of the earlier line lengths plus 1 per newline, and a line is a header if re.match of the given regex succeeds on it (case-sensitive; leading whitespace allowed by the regex's \s*). A row counts if at least one header line starts at offset >= L/2 and none starts at offset < L/2. Statistic = counted / kept. Bootstrap is over kept rows (0/1 flags). Refuted_by is coded as measured < 0.10. If no row is kept, the script prints not_computable, because the recipe does not say that an empty group refutes. Other reading (alt_measured): the length filter on n_new instead of n_generated. Possible errors: the text includes the prefilled cue, which has no header, so it does not matter. The regex also matches lines such as 'Example: ' or 'Question.' that are not textbook blocks, and it misses headers written as markdown ('**Problem 2:**') or as '### Solution'. The recipe is applied literally.

File: the base cue job abaybektursun-1114-151534-e72c answers.jsonl (stored at runs/theory-tests/). It has 328 rows, one per problem. Rows with a missing or null score_v3 are dropped (none were seen; every score_v3 is an int). Kept rows have cap_hit is False, score_v3 == 1 (the stored v3 score; it is not regraded) and n_generated > 10000 (strictly greater). r is computed as in prediction 1, and the statistic is the median of r over kept rows (mean of the two middle values for an even count). If no row qualifies, the script prints refuted_without_number, as the recipe says. Refuted_by is coded as measured > 0.92. Bootstrap is the median over resampled kept rows. Other reading (alt_measured): n_new > 10000 instead of n_generated. Possible errors: right, finished answers over 10,000 tokens are probably few, so the median may rest on a handful of rows with a wide interval. The recipe has no minimum row count, so the number is reported whatever n is.
